texto: Pedro Gallino plants a seedbed of mandarin trees at the La Amarilla estate, near today's Rodó Obelisk, from seeds brought from Rio de Janeiro by José Gonçalvez Amorim. These seedlings are believed to have started the region's first citrus groves.
fuente: Museo del Hombre y la Tecnología de Salto; Padrón Favre (2008)

titulo: The first harvest reaches the president
texto: A crate of oranges from the first harvest is sent to the President of Uruguay, José Ellauri: an early sign of the region's potential.
Italian immigrants help shape the farming, the community and the landscape of the citrus region.
Pedro Benito Solari champions planting orange trees along the streets of Salto, offering trees for the city. The idea later spreads to the towns of Belén and Constitución.

titulo: New know-how and the first exports
texto: Pedro Benito Solari brings back knowledge from research stations in Riverside, California, and Florida, introduces the Valencia orange and seedless mandarins, and leads the first exports of Salto oranges to Europe, selling them during the northern hemisphere's off-season.
fuente: Carlos Orihuela, interviewed by El Pueblo (2021); Archivo Isidra Solari

texto: New growers and companies, including the Caputto family, strengthen trade and exports from the region.
Uruguay's Ministry of Livestock, Agriculture and Fisheries organises the sector, steers small growers towards exports and sets quality standards.
The Citrícola Salteña packing house, designed by engineer Eladio Dieste, is built on Paraguay Avenue: about 4,200 m² under 17 double-curvature vaults of reinforced brick, spanning 45 metres.

Seedless, easy-peel mandarins, digital traceability, a cold chain for sea voyages of more than 30 days and constant watch against HLB (citrus greening). Uruguay's northern region holds about 91% of the country's citrus land.
